audio_caption: The audio clip begins with a female speaker describing atomic physics as the field of physics studying atoms, their atomic nucleus, and electron systems. She speaks in an informative tone, explaining that it mainly deals with how electrons are arranged around the nucleus and how they change. She adds that it also includes the atom's energy states and how it interacts with outside particles and electromagnetic fields. She concludes by saying that atomic physics is one of the most successful applications of quantum mechanics.

The audio begins with a male speaker discussing atomic theory, referencing ancient Greek philosophers like "Leucippus, Democritus." The speaker describes the atomic school's idea that "matter is made of very small, indivisible, and indestructible atoms," which were seen as continuously moving and colliding. The tone is informative and somewhat academic. The speaker then mentions "voids between the atoms" and questions the atomists could not answer.

The audio clip features a single male speaker discussing the history of the idea of the atom, mentioning Aristotle and his rejection of the atomic theory in favor of a continuous matter idea, and noting that the atom wasn't championed again until Lucretius. The speaker has an informative tone.

The audio clip features a single male speaker reading about scientific discoveries and theories, starting with, "In 17, Sir Isaac Newton showed that..." and discussing concepts like Boyle's Law, Dalton's atomic theory, and Avogadro's hypothesis, in a neutral and informative tone. There is no music, background sounds, or other identifiable sounds present.

The clip starts with a female speaker discussing 19th-century chemistry, mentioning ideas about finite elements and atom combinations in chemical compounds. Her tone is informative. This transitions to the mention of kinetic theory and the origin of pressure and viscosity in atomic motion. I'm unsure of what this sound is.

The audio features a male voice speaking in an informative tone about the atomic model. He begins by introducing the "plum pudding model" and describes the Rutherford gold foil experiment. He further explains how the experiment disproved the model due to the scattering patterns of alpha particles. Finally, he describes Rutherford's model of the atom, noting that the atom is mostly empty space. The background remains quiet throughout the speech.

The audio begins with a male speaker discussing the limitations of the planetary model of the atom. He explains how electrons would fall into the nucleus if they stood still, and how this led to a solar system model. The speaker mentions that the problems with the model helped lead to quantum mechanics. Throughout the speech, the tone is educational and explanatory.

The audio begins with a single male speaker explaining a problem with the planetary model, stating that "electrons are charged particles" and emit light, causing them to "spiral into the nucleus". The speaker speaks in an informative tone. He then mentions this led to the "four atomic model". The speaker continues, stating that "particles, such as electrons, have wavelike properties". Finally, the audio ends with a single-word utterance, "Okay."

The clip begins with a single female speaker, possibly reading from a script, discussing "de Broglie" and his demonstration of "waves" being bent into orbits, like "an electron". Her tone is informative and somewhat academic. She further explains that "electrons can only occupy those orbits" with a "whole number of wavelengths". The speaker then discusses how "constructive interference" allows waves to add together in those orbits, contrasting this with "fractional number of wavelengths" which would destructively interfere, preventing an electron from occupying such an orbit.

The audio clip begins with a male speaker discussing electron jumps, the emission of photons when going to a lower orbit, and the absorption of photons when going to a higher orbit. The speaker has an even tone, continuing to explain that the transitions match spectral lines in hydrogen, which was a major step in developing quantum mechanics.

The audio clip features one female speaker discussing the development of electron orbitals through the study of elements beyond hydrogen. She describes electron orbitals as places in an atom where electrons can be found and explains that their shapes were originally found mathematically. The speaker notes a historical view of these orbitals as mathematical abstractions and describes how field emission electron microscopy changed this view. She then describes images of both S and P orbitals. The speaker concludes that the imaging of these actual orbitals was surprising and shows the accuracy of the quantum atomic model and quantum mechanics as a whole.

The audio begins with a single female speaker discussing electron configuration, in a clear and somewhat educational tone. She provides an example of an electron configuration. This is followed by her discussing atomic spectra, explaining that it results from electrons changing atomic or molecular orbitals, fully explained by the quantum atomic model. The speaker then summarizes that atomic physics studies electrons around the atomic nucleus, how they are arranged and how those arrangements change. She concludes by stating that the understanding of the atom took over 2000 years to develop, but has provided many benefits. The audio ends with the sound of an electronic keyboard playing a drawn-out chord.
